sheet.howExamined: M3 (calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks). Almost always 3 marks, often as part (b) of a mensuration question: Summer 2025 Q19 asked for the volume of a cylinder and then the force from a pressure of 0.3 N/cm², and November 2025 Q25 set two solids at equal pressures. The scheme is MA1 for the area in contact, MA1 for the substitution, A1 for the value. The same pairing appears on M4 (Summer 2025 Q6, November 2025 Q10).
traps: Dividing the force by a volume, a total surface area or a single length instead of the area in contact (November 2025 M3 Q25 and M4 Q10)
Feeding the answer from the previous part, usually a volume, straight into the pressure formula (Summer 2025 M3 Q19, M4 Q6)
Turning the formula upside down: area ÷ force instead of force ÷ area
Dividing a square's area by 4 instead of square-rooting it (November 2025 M3 Q25 and M4 Q10)
Mixing units: an area in cm² with a pressure in N/m², when 1 m² = 10 000 cm²
Using the diameter as the radius for a circular base (Summer 2025 M4 Q6)
Missing a rounding instruction on the answer line (Summer 2025 M4 Q6)

whyMenu.explain: Pressure is how concentrated the push is. Spread the same force over a bigger contact patch and the pressure drops; that is why snowshoes work.

options: Because F is divided by A in the formula, so multiplying by A undoes it
Because force and area are always multiplied
Because pressure is a kind of force
whyMenu.explain: Undo the division. If P = F ÷ A then multiplying both sides by A leaves F on its own.

steps.decision: The pressure is per square centimetre and the area is in square centimetres, so they match and the answer comes out in newtons.
Areas convert by the square of the length factor. There are 100 cm in a metre, so there are $100^2 = 10\,000$ cm² in a square metre.

options: Because a square metre is 100 cm by 100 cm
Because area units always divide by 100
whyMenu.explain: Draw the square: 100 cm along each side gives 100 × 100 = 10 000 small squares of 1 cm².

steps.decision: The same force, as it must be. Converting both quantities consistently is the check that a unit change has been done properly.

options.feedback: Yes. From P = F ÷ A, multiply by A and divide by P.

items.stem: A pressure is given as 2500 N/m². What is that in pascals?

parts.stem:
A concrete cube of side 8 cm rests on a patio and presses down with a force of 640 N.

A planter with a square base rests on the same patio and presses down with a force of 250 N. The two objects exert the same pressure on the patio.

Calculate the length of one side of the planter's square base.
hints: Only the base of the cube touches the patio.
Find the cube's pressure, then use it for the planter.
A square's side is the square root of its area.
parts.workedSolution:
The cube rests on one face, so the area in contact is $8^2 = 64$ cm². Its pressure is $\dfrac{640}{64} = 10$ N/cm².

The planter has the same pressure, so its base area is $\dfrac{250}{10} = 25$ cm². The base is a square, so each side is $\sqrt{25} = 5.0$ cm.

commonErrors.feedback: The pressure and the planter's area are both right, so three marks stand. A square of area 25 cm² has side √25; dividing by 4 is the move for a perimeter.
The cube's pressure has been found by dividing by 512, its volume. Only one face touches the patio, so the area in contact is 64 cm² and the pressure is 10 N/cm².
The cube's pressure has been found by dividing by 384, all six faces. Five of them touch only air, so use the one face resting on the patio.

findTheMistake.stem: A metal cube of side 4 cm rests on a bench and presses down with a force of 480 N. Ruairí was asked for the pressure on the bench. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 works out the volume of the cube, 64 cm³. Pressure compares the force with the area that is actually touching the bench, and that is one square face, 4 × 4 = 16 cm².
findTheMistake.feedback: No marks, because the wrong quantity was measured, but the repair is one line long: write "area in contact = ..." before the formula. The November 2025 report on M4 Q10 said this in as many words — the difficulty was not the formula but deciding which area is in contact. The unit is another warning: cm³ under a force cannot give a pressure in N/cm².

findTheMistake.stem: A crate with a square base presses on the ground with a force of 320 N and a pressure of 5 N/cm². Aoife was asked for the length of one side of the base. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The area is found correctly and earns both method marks. Line 2 divides by 4, which is what you would do to a perimeter. A square of area 64 cm² has sides of $\sqrt{64}$ cm, because side × side gives the area.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks stand for the area. The check line is what catches it: square your answer and see whether the area comes back. In November 2025 this appeared on M3 Q25 and again on M4 Q10, and dividing by four instead of square-rooting was the step that cost the final mark both times.

prompts.prompt: Write the pressure formula, and its two rearrangements.
prompts.answer: Pressure = force ÷ area; force = pressure × area; area = force ÷ pressure.

prompts.prompt: Which area goes into the pressure formula?
prompts.answer: The area in contact with the surface — the face that is actually touching. Not the total surface area, and never the volume.
One newton per square metre. 1 Pa = 1 N/m², so a pressure in N/m² is already in pascals.

prompts.prompt: How many square centimetres are in a square metre?
prompts.answer: 10 000, because a square metre is 100 cm by 100 cm. To change cm² to m², divide by 10 000.

prompts.prompt: A square base has area 64 cm². How do you find its side, and why not divide by 4?
prompts.answer: Take the square root: √64 = 8 cm, because side × side gives the area. Dividing by 4 is what you would do to a perimeter.

prompts.prompt: Two objects exert the same pressure. How do you find an unknown base area?
prompts.answer: Work out the pressure from the object you know everything about, then use area = force ÷ pressure on the other one.

prompts.prompt: A question asks for the force from a pressure, just after a part that asked for a volume. What must you not do?
prompts.answer: Do not feed the volume into the pressure formula. Go back for the area in contact; the reports note that many candidates reuse the previous answer instead.

findings.asked: Surface area of a cylinder, then the force from its pressure on the floor.
findings.wentWrong: Many confused surface area with volume; a third got part (a); few connected area, pressure and force, and many fed their part (a) answer into part (b).
findings.rule: Force = pressure x area of the face touching the floor.

findings.asked: Volume of a cylinder, then the force it exerts on the floor.
findings.wentWrong: The volume was fine (some used r = 12 for a diameter of 12); many used that volume in the force calculation, and some missed the rounding instruction.
findings.rule: Pressure uses the contact area, never the volume.

findings.asked: Equal pressures from two solids; find the base edge of a square-based pyramid.
findings.wentWrong: Many got the cube's pressure but then divided the force by a length, a volume or a surface area (5, 125, 150) instead of the base area; those who reached the area often divided by 4 rather than square-rooting to get the edge.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Pressure = 560 / (base area of the cube), set equal to force / base area of the pyramid, solved for the area, then square-rooted.
findings.rule: Side of a square = square root of its area.

findings.asked: The same pressure problem on M4.
findings.wentWrong: Many started with the cube's volume and scored nothing; the final step of dividing by four instead of square-rooting recurred. The report's diagnosis: too much focus on the formula, too little on which area is in contact.
findings.rule: Write 'area in contact = ...' before you use the formula.

insight.ruleToRemember: Pressure = force / area of the face in contact; state which face and its area before calculating; a square's side is the square root of its area.
